subject: Biology
title: The Living World
summary: Living organisms grow, reproduce, metabolise, respond to their surroundings and are made of cells. Metabolism, cellular organisation and consciousness are the defining features; growth and reproduction alone are not.

Over 1.7–1.8 million species have been described. To study them, biologists name (nomenclature), identify, classify and arrange them in a hierarchy — this is taxonomy; systematics adds evolutionary relationships.
Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus) gives each organism a two-part scientific name: generic name + specific epithet, e.g. Mangifera indica.
Taxonomic categories run from kingdom down to species; each step down groups organisms that share more characters.

formulas.name: Defining features of life
formulas.formula: metabolism + cellular organisation + consciousness (response to stimuli)
formulas.mistake: Growth and reproduction are not defining: crystals grow, and mules or worker bees don't reproduce.

formulas.name: Binomial nomenclature
formulas.formula: Genus (capital first letter) + species (small letter), italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten, followed by the author's name (abbreviated)
formulas.mistake: Mangifera indica Linn. — the author's name is written in roman (not italics).

formulas.name: Taxonomic hierarchy
formulas.formula: Kingdom → Phylum (animals) / Division (plants) → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
formulas.note: Going up the hierarchy, the number of shared characters decreases.

formulas.name: Species
formulas.formula: a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring

formulas.name: Mango classification
formulas.formula: Plantae → Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera → indica

formulas.name: Human classification
formulas.formula: Animalia → Chordata → Mammalia → Primata → Hominidae → Homo → sapiens

formulas.name: Housefly and wheat
formulas.formula: housefly: Insecta → Diptera → Muscidae → Musca domestica;  wheat: Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Triticum aestivum

formulas.name: Taxonomic aids
formulas.formula: herbarium (dried, pressed plant specimens);  botanical garden (living plants);  museum (preserved specimens);  zoological park (live animals);  key (identification by contrasting couplets)

formulas.name: Taxonomic key
formulas.formula: based on couplets of contrasting characters (lead); separate keys for each category

formulas.name: Famous gardens
formulas.formula: Royal Botanical Gardens, Kew (England);  Indian Botanical Garden, Howrah;  National Botanical Research Institute, Lucknow

examples.title: Living or not?
examples.problem: Why is reproduction not considered a defining property of life?
examples.solution: Many living organisms cannot reproduce (mules, sterile worker bees, infertile humans), yet they are alive. Metabolism and cellular organisation are present in every living organism.

examples.title: Correct scientific name
examples.problem: Which is written correctly: Mangifera Indica, mangifera indica, Mangifera indica?
examples.solution: Mangifera indica — genus starts with a capital letter, the specific epithet with a small letter, both italicised.

examples.title: Shared characters
examples.problem: Which has more characters in common: members of a genus or members of a family?
examples.solution: Members of a genus. Lower categories group organisms that are more closely related, so they share more characters.

examples.title: Herbarium sheet
examples.problem: What information does a herbarium sheet carry?
examples.solution: The plant's scientific name, family, collector's name, date and place of collection, local name and field notes, along with the pressed specimen.

examples.title: Order vs family
examples.problem: Arrange family, order, genus and class from highest to lowest.

topics.title: Diversity in the living world
topics.explain: Biodiversity is the number and types of organisms on Earth. Local names differ from place to place, so scientific names are needed that are unique and accepted worldwide. At the highest level, life is grouped into three domains (Carl Woese): Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

topics.title: Nomenclature codes
topics.explain: Plant names follow the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN); animal names follow the International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN). Scientific names are Latin or Latinised.

topics.title: Growth and metabolism
topics.explain: In living organisms growth is from inside (increase in mass and number of cells). Metabolism is the sum of all chemical reactions in the body; isolated metabolic reactions in a test tube are not living.

topics.title: Taxonomy and systematics
topics.explain: Taxonomy: characterisation, identification, nomenclature and classification. Systematics (Linnaeus, Systema Naturae) also considers evolutionary relationships.

topics.title: Taxonomic categories
topics.explain: Each category (rank) is called a taxon. The hierarchy has seven obligate categories; intermediate ranks like sub-species or super-family are sometimes used.

topics.title: Museums, zoos and keys
topics.explain: Museums keep animals in preservative solutions and as skins or skeletons; insects are pinned in boxes. Zoological parks keep wild animals in protected surroundings like their natural habitats. Flora, manuals, monographs and catalogues also help identification.
